sections.h2: Who settles landlord and tenant disputes
sections.html:
No state agency does. Georgia has no government office with power to step into a rental dispute or compel either side to act. People who cannot settle a disagreement go to court, on their own or with a lawyer.

The Department of Community Affairs hosts a Landlord-Tenant Handbook, which Georgia State University and the University of Georgia have edited and updated since 2021. English and Spanish PDFs are posted. A seller with a tenant in the house, or an owner thinking about renting one out, can use it as a plain-language baseline for the points below.

A landlord may not demand more than two months of rent as a deposit. Owners of more than ten rental units, counting units held by a spouse or children, and owners who hire a management agent face extra duties.

  • Deposits go into a bank escrow account used only for that purpose, or the owner posts a bond with the superior court clerk. Tenants get written notice of where the money sits.
  • Before accepting a deposit, the owner hands over a written list of existing damage, lets the tenant check it, and both sides sign.
  • After a lease ends, the landlord has three business days, or a reasonable time after learning the tenant left, to inspect and list damage with estimated costs.

The tenant may inspect during the first five business days after termination and should sign the list or write down what is disputed. A tenant who gave proper notice and owes nothing is entitled to the deposit back within thirty days. Ordinary wear and tear cannot be charged against it.

sections.h2: When the owner sells a rental
sections.html:
The deposit travels with the sale. The former owner either passes it to the new owner, who then answers for it, or returns it to the tenant. A tenant left without either can sue, and it helps to write to both owners first to ask about the money.

The lease itself generally stays in place too. An apartment complex that changes hands is usually bound by existing leases, so new owners cannot raise rent or alter rules mid-term. A seller handing over an occupied rental should give the buyer the signed lease, the deposit amount and the move-in damage list. Gathering those three items before listing saves a scramble at closing.

sections.h2: Notice to end a month-to-month tenancy
sections.html:
A landlord needs to give sixty days, and a tenant needs to give thirty. This arrangement is called a tenancy-at-will, and it also requires sixty days' notice before a changed rent amount takes hold.

Common notice and response periods
SituationPeriodWho acts
Landlord ends a tenancy-at-will60 daysLandlord
Tenant ends a tenancy-at-will30 daysTenant
New rent for a tenant-at-will60 daysLandlord
Leaving early with a court protection order30 daysTenant
Reply to an eviction summons7 days from serviceTenant
Tender of rent and court costs, usable once per 12 months7 days after serviceTenant

Fixed-term leases run by their own wording, and a landlord filing for eviction must follow that wording on notice and termination.

A tenant can leave early only on the lease's terms, with narrow exceptions for service members relocating on orders and tenants fleeing family violence. A tenant who abandons the unit without a lawful reason may owe the landlord money.

Early termination fees are allowed when three conditions hold: the landlord's loss is hard to estimate, both sides meant the fee to cover damages and not to punish, and the amount is a reasonable estimate. If the tenant leaves without permission, the landlord is not required to find a new tenant. The unit can sit empty while the tenant stays on the hook for rent through the end of the lease, unless the landlord accepts the departure.

Foreclosure ends the original landlord-tenant relationship, and the lender or new owner can pursue an eviction. A tenant is not removed automatically, and a new owner may choose to set up a fresh arrangement. An owner who wants the tenant out still has to give notice.

One trap: if a new owner has started eviction proceedings and then takes or asks for rent, a valid tenancy-at-will can result. Everyone involved should keep written notices.

A rental must be kept safe, habitable and in good repair. That means maintaining the building structure, keeping electric, heating, cooling and plumbing working, and using ordinary care to keep the unit safe.

A lease cannot excuse those duties or declare that the landlord need not follow local laws or Georgia's deposit rules. Tenants should report problems promptly, in writing if possible and in the manner the lease requires. Problems that were obvious at move-in are usually the tenant's, unless they make the unit unsafe or uninhabitable.

Retaliation for repair requests or code complaints is unlawful. Filing for eviction, reducing services or raising rent soon afterward is presumed retaliatory unless the landlord shows a lawful reason, such as unpaid rent or serious lease violations.

It begins with a demand for possession. The demand does not have to be written unless the reason is unpaid rent, and no special words are needed. The landlord then files a dispossessory affidavit, most often in magistrate court, though state, superior and some municipal courts can hear one.

After service, the tenant has seven days to answer, and the answer should include every defense and counterclaim. Without an answer the court can order the tenant out and send the sheriff.

  • In a nonpayment case, paying the full alleged amount plus court costs within seven days stops the eviction, but only once in a twelve-month stretch.
  • If the landlord will not take the money, the tenant says so in the answer.
  • A court finding a proper offer can require the landlord to accept payment made within three days of its ruling.

Courts may require or suggest mediation before the hearing. A mediator does not decide the case.

sections.h2: Fair housing, lead paint and squatters
sections.html:
Fair housing law protects classes including race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status and disability, and a landlord must allow reasonable accommodations for tenants with disabilities.

Owners renting units built before 1978 must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards in the unit and common areas unless a state-certified inspector finds none. A squatter is someone who never had the owner's permission to enter. The owner can swear an affidavit to have that person removed without an eviction case, and the squatter may face criminal penalties. People who stay past a lease are covered by the dispossessory steps above.

Free legal help comes from the Georgia Legal Services Program, Atlanta Legal Aid Society in Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, Gwinnett and Clayton counties, and georgialegalaid.org.

faqs.q: Can a Georgia landlord charge a deposit of three months' rent?
faqs.a: No. A landlord cannot require a security deposit worth more than two months of rent.

faqs.q: Does a tenant have to leave when the landlord sells the house?
faqs.a: Not automatically. New owners are generally subject to existing leases, and a tenant-at-will is owed sixty days of notice from the landlord.

faqs.q: How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in Georgia?
faqs.a: Thirty days when the tenant gave proper notice and left owing nothing. Normal wear and tear cannot be deducted.

faqs.q: Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying what is owed?
faqs.a: Yes, in nonpayment cases, if the tenant pays the alleged rent, fees and court costs within seven days of service. This works once in any twelve-month period.

faqs.q: Who can I call for free help with a rental dispute?
faqs.a: The Georgia Legal Services Program covers most of the state, and Atlanta Legal Aid Society serves Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, Gwinnett and Clayton counties. Georgialegalaid.org has self-help guides.
